meta.title: Vetted AI code is hard to justify
meta.author: amoffat

comments.author: creesch
comments.text:
about a week to comprehend the massive diff it produced


It is insane to me that models aren't better trained on this and the harnesses don't default to better practices. But you do not need to have one massive diff. There are skill plugins like superpowers that attempt to let these models/harnesses make use of good practices like TDD, DRY, etc and they actually do improve the quality output in a remarkable way and give you much better structured commits.

Most people I know who use AI somewhat successfully in their workflow have had to spend A LOT of time putting up a ton of skill scaffolding and other instructions before they got to that point. Some of that comes down to project specific idiosyncrasies but a majority from what I have seen is the same sort of stuff as the superpowers skill set, trying to get these things to follow basic fundamental software development practices.

As I said, it is borderline insane to me that none of the frontier labs includes those practices themselves in their harnesses or model training to any significant degree as far as I can tell. They all seem to focus on the sort of quick idea to code type development that works for prototypes but falls apart for larger projects.

And to be extra clear, even with these skills in place it still is exhausting to me to use agentic coding with harnesess like claude code. But if your work requires you to use them or you want to actually trial them, do yourself a favor and at least try and use something like superpowers to get some semblance of sanity in the flow.

Now to get back to the article. I find the contrast between "using AI is extremely exhausting" and "Also, here is an interactive representation I had the AI make" pretty hilarious to be honest.

comments.author: hobbified
comments.text:
As I said, it is borderline insane to me that none of the frontier labs includes those practices themselves in their harnesses or model training to any significant degree as far as I can tell.


A couple weeks ago I started a project with Claude. Not my first one, but this is the first one that feels "really big" to me (sending pictures over HF radio using an OFDM modem and a neural codec trained with a differentiable channel simulator in the training loop). And I got some pretty nice behavior out of it without having to prompt it specifically. I just opened up plan mode on an empty repo and asked for a design and a prototype for something that does XYZ, giving it the concept, the constraints, and some reading on the closest related prior art (FreeDV RADE). After asking some questions to firm up the spec, it decided on a config.py that encoded all of the important numbers from the spec as constants and derived everything else from that. It decided on a nicely layered design with an implementation plan to match, and it decided on way more rigorous testing than I would have had patience for while doing something experimental, so that everything about the modem is asserted, from the simple fact that it does get data across, to its SNR and frequency-offset tolerances being at least as wide as what the spec asked for. Pretty much every requirements clarification or bug found results in a new test. And when I told it I wanted to port the app to C++ it came up with a plan where each Python module has a corresponding C++ module, there are tests that directly assert equivalence between Python and C++ versions, and there are tests that substitute one implementation for another at module boundaries and have to pass both ways.

It's been a crazy trip and of course not without a few mistakes, but the damn thing works far better than I ever thought it would, the code quality is not crap, the commit history is tolerable, and I've actually learned a few things along the way, about both modem design and software design. My biggest complaint is that the documentation and the code comments are both somewhat overly-verbose with qualifications and justifications, a lot of which feel already obsolete by the time they're written down. I push back on some of that (especially when it invents justifications based on completely imaginary user behavior patterns) but I let a lot of it ride because it really does help with not making the same mistake twice.

comments.author: creesch
comments.text:
I have had a similar experience as you with some projects, but not all projects.
Green field projects, certainly at the start will likely yield you the best initial results. But, it highly depends on the framing of the prompt as well. Over a longer period of time over the same project I saw it would sometimes apply rigorous practices on small things while completely skipping any best practices for some more complex things.

So in my experience it is wildly inconsistent in how Claude will apply some development practices at times or if it will even apply them.

Basically, these practices are clearly somewhere in the training data, certainly more recently. But the way the surface very much gives me a strong feeling that they are still an afterthought.

comments.author: orib
comments.text:
The bottleneck for producing code understanding what it is you're building. Typing it out is a small part of the work. Therefore, the way to realize the benefits of AI development is skipping the time it takes to build theory around the code.

It may even work sometimes. As long as you don't mind the massive societal consequences.

comments.author: FPGAhacker
comments.text: I'm not so sure it's fair to say typing it out is a small part of the work.  People think in different ways, some blog, some walk around and ponder, others verbalize and gesticulate.  Is it so crazy to believe some people think by writing out code?

comments.author: orib
comments.text: I think you missed the point. I don't many people are bottlenecked by typing speed, but by building understanding.

comments.author: k749gtnc9l3w
comments.text: When understanding is built by writing out code and checking things with that code, I would indeed say that typing speed is the bottleneck for that process of building understanding. Sometimes it is instead finding which section of documentation is the one relevant to the currently needed detail.

comments.author: orib
comments.text: So you're suggesting that maybe you can get a large speedup on coding speed by finding methods of building understanding that need less typing, with no changes to how you write the shipped code. Interesting.

comments.author: k749gtnc9l3w
comments.text:
You cannot understand behaviour of unreliable counterparties without poking at them, that's a myth.

You cannot truly evaluate the success rate of auto-cleanups of garbage data without test runs.

That's the problem, there is code where finding a meaningfully more concise way (fewer lexer-tokens; autocompletion of long names works fine even just as vim's Ctrl-n) is a lot of effort, and possibly some overhead when working with it later; and if you don't try to go this deadly way, then thinking part is trivial but low quality generator gives something faster which is already useful enough. This might be understanding-building probing or preparing final code.

Speaking of shipped, I use daily some ultra-personalised local-LLM-generated code. Some of it, even for interacting with Lobste.rs. Yeah, I needed to debug it, both faster and more interesting than writing this ultra-straightforward stuff. Also both faster and less absurd-feeling than golfing it and then fighting the corner cases. LLM generated a list of cases almost correctly, and fixing the mistakes in the long-form list was quick enough. (I consider it a complicated question in which cases generated output is how much of partial plagiarism of training data — but there are cases where I would use other things with questionable plagiarism status anyway without much hesitation)

I define enough macros in my Common Lisp code, and I have worked with enough garbage data, not to believe the talk about universality of search more concise ways of expressing things, and about there always being something to understand without poking a lot of times at the thing.

comments.author: orib
comments.text: I definitely write a bunch of code to poke at things, but I spend a lot more time staring at the output with a notebook and paper than I do writing that code. The bottleneck, at least for me, isn't the typing.

comments.author: k749gtnc9l3w
comments.text:
The real time bottleneck is often checking the documentation «do they actually promise anything at all about that or really not».

I would say that typing out large chunks of simple stuff is in fact a bottleneck for me, if not in time, then at least in the sense of where I can run out of energy slowing things down. This even applies to writing some of the theoretical CS articles.

comments.author: n1000
comments.text:
This is a nice way to partition LLM-assisted work into segments based on practical and psychological toll but I find the "dashboard" to be confusing. It's hard to understand all of the sliders without mousing over the tooltips and it's not clear what's happening when you drag one of the sliders and (e.g.) the y-axis scale shifts.

I believe the piece would be stronger as a longer essay without the interactive bit. Perhaps you could write brief paragraphs explaining the different quadrants regimes (I don't know the actual number) that the reader now has to search for by manually searching the 4-dimensional parameter space.

comments.author: Yogthos
comments.text:
about a week to comprehend the massive diff it produced


I mean here's your problem. Instead of having the LLM crap out one massive change, spend some time breaking the task up. Then have the LLM produce small focused deliverables as pull requests, and review them individually. This is no different from how you'd work on a feature on a team as well I might add. Nobody wants to see massive PRs that conflate a bunch of features together. There's absolutely no reason to let the agent churn out a bunch of code before you look at it.

comments.author: tobin_baker
comments.text: I use the superpowers plugin and ask the agent to plan a series of stacked diffs, just like we used to do before LLMs. Each diff it produces is easily reviewable on its own.

comments.author: Yogthos
comments.text: Yup, I also like using Mermaid diagrams during planning to break up the task into pieces and review how they connect to each other. I find it helps a lot to express control logic as a state machine, and then each step can be implemented as its own task in isolation.

comments.author: amoffat
comments.text: This is good advice for engineers who are "conflating a bunch of features together," but this is not one of those problems.

comments.author: Yogthos
comments.text: Could you give a bit more detail to explain what makes the complexity irreducible in this case? Or were you breaking things up into step and talking about overall volume of review needed?

comments.author: amoffat
comments.text: The problem that I am seeing is less that the feature cannot be broken into smaller pieces, and more that reviewing a nontrivial amount of smart-but-sometimes-very-flawed code has a high burnout multiplier. It feels genuinely different than a human teammate because all of the ownership falls on me, versus being shared with the teammate.

comments.author: Yogthos
comments.text: How do you end up having to review nontrivial amount of smart-but-sometimes-very-flawed code is the part I'm curious about. My process has been to sketch out a high level solution, then have the agent produce a mermaidjs diagram I can review, and then create a phased implementation plan based on that. The model then uses TDD to implement each phase, and by the time tests pass, the code tends to be fine. I basically treat the tests as a contract the model has to fill.

comments.author: Student
comments.text: I’m not sure this is hard to justify? It’s hard because it’s exercising your brain in a way quite different from writing your own code, but it’s still twice as fast as the estimate. It’s possibly better tested and verified as well.

comments.author: kingmob
comments.text:
Yeah, I thought the speed of implementation kind of undercut the headline a bit.

There's a lot of areas where pursuing speed over things like quality or understanding is a valid trade-off. (Many startups have done exactly this for decades before AI.)

comments.author: abeyer
comments.text: Doesn't really contradict the point on burnout... startups have also been a notorious place for engineers to burn themselves out doing so.

comments.author: kingmob
comments.text:
Agreed, but that's not the part we're talking about.

The headline says "Vetted AI code is hard to justify", but the article admits that the implementation was faster than if it had been hand-written. Releasing faster at the cost of other attributes (maintainability, code quality, developer health, etc) is justifiable in a general sense.

We're all stuck under capitalism, and there are frequently advantages to being first to market.
